title: Discrete-Time Signal Processing, MIT 6.341, Fall 2005 — shard 2: Lectures 9–16, Problem Sets 5–8, and Midterm
access: Full access to the assigned MIT-published corpus through official MIT OpenCourseWare resource pages. Read: lecture notes for Lectures 9–13 and 15–16; Problem Sets 5–8 and all four solutions; Fall 2005 midterm and solution. Lecture 14 (guest lecture by Gene Frantz) is listed in the schedule but has no posted note PDF, so no content is inferred for it. MIT OCW states CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 except where otherwise noted.
topics: Lecture 9, pp. 1–3 — FIR design by windowing: mean-square optimal truncation, frequency-domain convolution, transition width versus sidelobe ripple, common windows, and the Kaiser family.

Lecture 9, pp. 3–6 — Optimum FIR approximation: generalized linear phase, Chebyshev-polynomial representation, the alternation theorem, equiripple properties, and the Parks–McClellan exchange algorithm.
Lecture 10, pp. 1–2 — Multirate motivation and review: equivalent systems with radically different multiplication rates; expander and compressor input-output and DTFT relations.
Lecture 10, pp. 2–5 — Downsampling noble identity, polyphase decomposition, movement of filtering to the low-rate side, and multiplication-rate accounting.
Lecture 11, pp. 1–3 — Upsampling noble identity, frequency-domain intuition, interpolation polyphase decomposition, and efficiency as a multidimensional design criterion.
Lecture 12, pp. 1–2 — Parametric signal modeling: model/error/optimization workflow, all-pole models, and prediction-error interpretation.
Lecture 12, pp. 2–4 — Deterministic and stochastic linear prediction, autocorrelation normal equations, Yule–Walker Toeplitz systems, and inverse whitening.
Lecture 13, pp. 1–5 — Levinson–Durbin derivation: order recursion from Toeplitz structure, correction vector, reflection coefficient, and summarized algorithm.
Lecture 13, pp. 5–6 — All-pole and all-zero lattice realizations, reflection-coefficient stability test, finite-precision advantages, and speech coding/synthesis relevance.
Lecture 14 — Guest lecture by Gene Frantz; no lecture-note PDF is posted in the official corpus and therefore no content was available to read.
Lecture 15, pp. 1–3 — Why the DTFT cannot be computed directly, frequency sampling, time aliasing by duality, and conditions for recovery from DTFT samples.
Lecture 15, pp. 3–6 — Discrete Fourier series, periodic convolution, DFT as the DFS of a periodic extension, circular shift/convolution, and the DTFT–DFS–DFT relationship.
Lecture 16, pp. 1–3 — Circular convolution as periodic convolution and as linear convolution followed by time aliasing.
Lecture 16, pp. 3–5 — DFT length for alias-free linear convolution, overlap-add, and overlap-save block filtering.

Problem Set 5 and solution — FIR design practice: truncation proof, continuous-to-discrete derivative approximations, alternation arguments, spectral factorization, multistage decimation design, and reconstruction compensation.
Problem Set 6 and solution — Multirate/polyphase practice: efficient structures, alias-cancellation filter banks, coprime rate changes, WSS output correlation, and second-order all-pole modeling.
Problem Set 7 and solution — Prediction-model mismatch, DFT transformations, symmetry, circular convolution, operation-cost selection, and an overlap-save filter defined by frequency samples.
Problem Set 8 and solution — Direct/recursive DFT computation, Goertzel structure, two-real-DFTs-through-one-complex-DFT, real-input FFT economy, and FFT block convolution sizing.

Fall 2005 Midterm and solution — Minimum-phase/all-pass decomposition; continuous/discrete multirate equivalence; lattice recursion; FIR-order inference from extrema; and DFT-domain compression/expansion duality.
key_results: For a desired impulse response hd[n], minimizing integral squared frequency error over causal FIR sequences supported on 0≤n≤M gives h[n]=hd[n] on that interval and zero elsewhere; by Parseval this is exactly rectangular truncation. [Lecture 9 p. 1; PS5 solution p. 1]

Windowing multiplies hd[n] in time and convolves Hd(e^jω) with W(e^jω) in frequency. Main-lobe width controls transition width, while sidelobe area controls passband/stopband ripple; increasing a rectangular window’s length narrows lobes but does not reduce ripple amplitude. [Lecture 9 pp. 1–2]

Smooth tapering trades a wider main lobe for lower sidelobes. Rectangular, Bartlett, Hann, Hamming, and Blackman windows are fixed choices; the Kaiser family exposes the tradeoff continuously through length M+1 and shape β. [Lecture 9 p. 2]

For Kaiser design with stopband attenuation A=-20log10δ, β is piecewise in A and the order estimate is M≥(A−8)/(2.285Δω); this turns ripple and transition specifications into a practical first design. [Lecture 9 p. 3]
A type-I generalized-linear-phase FIR filter has symmetric h[n], even M, and H(e^jω)=Ae(e^jω)e^(−jωM/2), where Ae is a degree-L=M/2 polynomial P(cosω). [Lecture 9 p. 4]

The alternation theorem certifies the unique minimax polynomial approximation: a degree-L optimum has at least L+2 alternating extrema of weighted error. The Parks–McClellan algorithm repeatedly solves at guessed extremals, evaluates on a dense grid, exchanges the extremals, and stops when they no longer move. [Lecture 9 pp. 4–6]

For a type-I optimum lowpass, alternations occur at both band edges, passband and stopband ripples are equal under equal weighting, and the transition is monotonic. A PS5 proof shows that any transition-band extremum consumes too many of the polynomial’s available extrema to satisfy alternation. [Lecture 9 p. 5; PS5 solution pp. 4–5]
For expansion by L, xe[n]=x[n/L] when n/L is integral and 0 otherwise, with Xe(e^jω)=X(e^jωL). For compression by M, xd[n]=x[nM] and Xd(e^jω)=(1/M)Σ(k=0 to M−1)X(e^j(ω−2πk)/M). [Lecture 10 p. 2]

The downsampling noble identity moves a filter H(z^M) across a compressor by M; the reverse direction is valid only when the high-rate filter can be written using integer powers of z^M. [Lecture 10 pp. 2–3]

Polyphase decomposition partitions h[n] into ek[n]=h[nM+k]. In a decimator, each branch can cross its compressor by the noble identity, putting every multiplication on the low-rate side without changing the input-output relation. [Lecture 10 pp. 3–5]

For an N-tap FIR preceding downsampling by M, direct filtering costs N multiplications per input-time second, whereas a polyphase low-rate implementation costs N/M under the lecture’s assumptions. [Lecture 10 pp. 4–5]
The upsampling noble identity supports the dual interpolation construction: decompose h[n] into L polyphase components and move all filters to the low-rate side of the expanders. [Lecture 11 pp. 2–3]

Efficiency is not a single scalar: moving multipliers to a low-rate side can reduce multiplies per second while adding expander blocks or delay storage. The notes explicitly require the designer to state what ‘efficient’ means. [Lecture 11 p. 2]

Parametric modeling follows three steps: choose a model and parameters, define a modeling error, and minimize it. The shard uses S-hat(z)=A/(1−Σ(k=1 to p)akz^−k), then defines error after the inverse model so optimization becomes linear. [Lecture 12 pp. 1–2]

For causal deterministic data, least-squares prediction gives the Yule–Walker equations Σ(k=1 to p)ak φs[i−k]=φs[i], i=1,…,p, or Tp ap=rp, with a symmetric Toeplitz autocorrelation matrix. [Lecture 12 pp. 3–4]

The same normal equations arise statistically when an all-pole model is driven by white noise and the inverse filter is chosen to whiten the observed process, replacing deterministic correlation by expectation. [Lecture 12 p. 4]

Levinson–Durbin obtains an order-(p+1) solution from the order-p solution by exploiting Toeplitz symmetry. With reversed correlation vector qp and coefficient vector ρp, kp+1=[φs[p+1]−qp^T ap]/[φs[0]−rp^T ap], the correction is −kp+1ρp, and the new final coefficient is kp+1. [Lecture 13 pp. 2–5]
The recursion starts at a1^(1)=φs[1]/φs[0], avoids a fresh matrix inversion at each order, and yields every lower-order model on the way to order p. [Lecture 13 pp. 2, 5]

The Levinson reflection coefficients directly parameterize all-pole/all-zero lattice realizations. If every |kα|<1, the all-pole lattice is stable—a convenient finite-precision test compared with explicitly finding direct-form poles. [Lecture 13 pp. 5–6]

Sampling a DTFT at N equally spaced frequencies produces X[k]=Σn x[n]W_N^(nk). Perfect recovery from those samples requires the signal’s occupied duration to fit within N samples; otherwise periodic replication causes time aliasing. [Lecture 15 pp. 1–3]

A period-N sequence needs only N distinct complex exponentials. Its DFS pair is X-tilde[k]=Σ(n=0 to N−1)x-tilde[n]W_N^(nk) and x-tilde[n]=(1/N)Σ(k=0 to N−1)X-tilde[k]W_N^(−nk), with both sequences periodic modulo N. [Lecture 15 pp. 3–4]

The N-point DFT of finite x[n] is the DFS of its period-N extension and equivalently samples its DTFT at ω=2πk/N. Choosing a different N, including zero padding, generally produces different DFT samples without changing the underlying DTFT. [Lecture 15 pp. 4–6]
A circular time shift x[((n−m))N] multiplies X[k] by exp(−j2πkm/N); multiplication of two DFTs corresponds to N-point circular convolution. [Lecture 15 p. 5]

N-point circular convolution equals linear convolution followed by periodic time aliasing into N samples. For sequences of lengths L and P, N≥L+P−1 makes circular and linear convolution agree. [Lecture 16 pp. 2–4]

Overlap-add filters nonoverlapping L-sample blocks using transforms of length at least L+P−1 and adds the P−1-sample overlaps. Overlap-save uses overlapping blocks, discards each block’s first P−1 aliased outputs, and retains the uncorrupted remainder. [Lecture 16 pp. 4–5]

Backward-Euler substitution s=(1−z^−1)/T maps the stable continuous-time left half-plane inside the unit circle, whereas forward Euler z=1+sT maps it left of Re(z)=1 and can turn a stable analog pole into an unstable digital pole. Both are accurate near ΩT≈0. [PS5 solution pp. 2–3]

A three-tap type-I minimax lowpass with passband edge π/3 and stopband edge π/2 is h[n]=(1/3)(δ[n]+δ[n−1]+δ[n−2]), obtained by forcing three alternating errors at π/3, π/2, and π. [PS5 solution pp. 4–5]

For a suitable even-order linear-phase equiripple FIR, adding the stopband ripple δ2 makes the zero-phase response nonnegative; spectral factorization assigns reciprocal zero pairs to a minimum-phase half-order factor, reducing length from M+1 to M/2+1 with transformed ripple bounds. [PS5 solution pp. 5–6]

A two-stage decimator can use a much wider first-stage transition band because later rate change and spectral periodicity relax its stopband edge. In the PS5 example, symmetry and low-rate computation cut steady-state work from 2535 to 284 multiplications per final output sample. [PS5 solution pp. 6–10]

In a two-channel analysis/synthesis bank with H1(e^jω)=H0(e^j(ω+π)), perfect delayed reconstruction for arbitrary stable input requires H0²(e^jω)+H1²(e^jω)=Kexp(−jndω) and H0(e^jω)H1(e^jω)=0. [PS6 solution pp. 1–3]

Expansion by 2, filtering by h[n], and compression by 2 reduces exactly to ordinary LTI filtering by the even polyphase component e0[n]=h[2n]; the odd branch receives only zeros. For white WSS input, Rdd[m]=σw²Σk h[2k]h[2(k+m)]. [PS6 solution p. 7]
Coprime expansion and compression factors commute. PS6 uses this plus a noble identity to collapse filtering expressed in z^6 onto the lowest-rate side. [PS6 solution pp. 5–6]

If a signal is exactly the impulse response of a second-order all-pole system, its p=2 Yule–Walker fit recovers the pole coefficients, and every coefficient added at p>2 is zero. [PS6 solution pp. 8–9]

Exact recurrence and global least-squares all-pole modeling are different: a sum of exponentials can obey a second-order recurrence after startup yet fail to be the impulse response of a pure all-pole system; then raising model order changes earlier optimum coefficients. [PS7 solution pp. 1–2]

Zero-padding a length-N sequence to 2N samples gives twice as dense samples of the same DTFT. Expanding in time by 2 instead produces a 2N-point DFT consisting of two repeats of the original N DFT samples. [PS7 solution pp. 6–7]

For a real sequence, X[k]=X*[N−k]; the DFT real part is circular-even and imaginary part circular-odd. This symmetry lets two real N-point DFTs be recovered from one complex N-point DFT. [PS8 solution pp. 3–5]

The Goertzel recursion yk[n]=x[n]+W_N^k yk[n−1] accumulates a selected bin; at n=N it yields X[N−k] under the problem’s convention. A second-order real resonator form follows by pairing conjugate factors. [PS8 solution pp. 1–2]
With length-128 blocks and a length-64 FIR, linear convolution has length 191; radix-2 FFT block filtering therefore pads both inputs to 256 points. [PS8 solution p. 6]

A stable rational system decomposes uniquely up to scale into a stable minimum-phase magnitude factor and stable all-pass factors by reflecting every outside-unit-circle zero to its conjugate reciprocal and using all-pass sections to restore the original phase/zeros. [Midterm solution pp. 2–3]

In the midterm’s C/D → expand-by-2 → H → compress-by-2 → D/C chain, the digital middle reduces to h[2n] with response (1/2)[H(e^jω/2)+H(e^j(ω/2−π))]. The overall CT system is LTI whenever sampling aliases are absent or rejected by that equivalent filter. [Midterm solution pp. 4–5]

Replacing z by z² in an FIR lattice inserts a zero-reflection stage before every original stage: expansion of h[n] by 2 maps original reflection coefficients to the even-numbered coefficients and sets odd-numbered ones to zero. [Midterm solution pp. 6–7]

An even FIR supported on −L≤n≤L is a degree-L polynomial in cosω and has at most L+1 extrema on [0,π]. Six visible extrema therefore imply L≥5 without assuming how the filter was designed. [Midterm solution pp. 8–9]

Compressing a 1024-point DFT by 2 aliases time: the 512-point IDFT is r[n]=x[n]+x[n+512]. Re-expanding those frequency samples by 2 repeats r[n] twice in time with factor 1/2. [Midterm solution pp. 10–11]
pedagogy: This is a compact graduate course corpus that alternates terse derivation notes with demanding problem sets and concise worked solutions. The lectures assume fluency with DTFT/z-transform algebra, LTI systems, sampling, complex numbers, matrix notation, and the Oppenheim–Schafer–Buck textbook; they frequently point to textbook figures rather than reproducing full explanations. New ideas begin with a provocative question or an operation-count comparison, then move through equations and block-diagram transformations. Problems require proofs, exact system transformations, spectrum sketches, operation counts, and implementation choices—not rote formula substitution. Problem Sets 5–8 comprise 31 numbered problems (including one optional item and textbook-referenced subproblems), with solutions that expose design reasoning and edge cases. The midterm is closed book with five synthesis problems and explicitly grades demonstrated understanding on an E/G/R/M/U scale; several later parts remain independently solvable. The strongest recurring pedagogy is to make students state the notion of efficiency, distinguish mathematically similar but operationally different transforms, and justify every equivalence by both algebra and signal-flow intuition.

gems: A design can be mathematically optimal and still be poor: rectangular truncation minimizes integrated squared error, yet its fixed-height ripple motivates a different minimax objective. [Lecture 9 pp. 1–3]

The notes turn window lore into two physical knobs: main-lobe width sets transition width; sidelobe mass sets ripple. A smoother endpoint buys smaller ripple by spending transition sharpness. [Lecture 9 p. 2]

‘What do we mean by efficient?’ is the multirate lecture’s comeback: a manipulation can reduce multiplications while increasing expander blocks, so the cost model must be named before optimization. [Lecture 11 p. 2]
An N-tap decimator goes from N to N/M multiplies per second simply by refusing to compute samples that the compressor will throw away. [Lecture 10 pp. 1, 4–5]

The sinusoid sampling riddle answers 0 Hz: a single sinusoid below 5 kHz has only amplitude, phase, and frequency as unknowns, so three nonuniform samples can identify it and no continuing sample stream is needed. It is deliberately surprising and opens parametric modeling. [Lecture 12 p. 1]

All-pole modeling replaces a nonlinear output mismatch with a convenient inverse-filter error; the freedom to choose the error criterion is what makes the normal equations appear. [Lecture 12 pp. 1–3]
Levinson–Durbin is presented as algebra with a structural payoff: intermediate recursion coefficients are not bookkeeping waste but the actual lattice reflection coefficients. [Lecture 13 pp. 1, 5–6]

The five opening DFT warnings are memorable: the DTFT cannot be computed, the DFT can, the DFT is not the DTFT, the FFT is not the DFT, and the FFT is not always the best way to compute its result. [Lecture 15 p. 1]

Putting a finite sequence around a cylinder makes periodic extension, circular shift, and circular convolution literal rotations and wraparound rather than abstract modulo arithmetic. [Lecture 15 p. 5; Lecture 16 pp. 3–4]
A same-looking signal assigned length 5 versus length 10 has different DFT values because the DFT samples a different grid and implies a different periodic extension. [Lecture 15 p. 5]

Overlap-save’s ‘corrupted but useful’ insight: circular convolution need not be globally alias-free; discard the first P−1 wrapped samples and keep the remaining L−P+1 exact samples. [Lecture 16 pp. 3–5]

The Euler mapping comparison gives a clean stability lesson: backward Euler preserves analog stability automatically, while forward Euler may not, even though both improve as T shrinks. [PS5 solution pp. 2–3]

A multistage-decimator design turns a 5069-tap-style burden into 284 multiplies per output by widening the early transition band, exploiting symmetry, and computing before samples are discarded only when necessary. [PS5 solution pp. 8–10]

A ‘near miss’ filter that is almost a function of z^6 becomes efficient by splitting off one awkward term in parallel; systematic polyphase decomposition reveals that several branches are exactly zero. [PS6 solution pp. 5–6]
Expansion-filter-compression can erase half a filter: after ↑2 and ↓2, the odd polyphase branch receives zero forever and the whole system is just h[2n]. [PS6 solution p. 7]

Two sums of exponentials expose a subtle modeling distinction: one is a pure two-pole impulse response and keeps its fitted coefficients at higher orders; the other has a numerator transient, so global least-squares coefficients keep changing even though its tail obeys the same recurrence. [PS6 solution pp. 8–9; PS7 solution pp. 1–2]

A 256-bin brick-wall mask inside overlap-save is not an ideal frequency-selective filter: its IDFT is finite, while a truly ideal frequency cutoff requires an infinite impulse response. [PS7 pp. 1–2; solution pp. 9–10]

The DFT transformation-matching exercise separates two operations often conflated: zero padding doubles frequency-grid density, while time expansion repeats the original frequency samples twice. [PS7 solution pp. 5–7]

Two real DFTs can hitchhike in one complex DFT by packing one sequence into the real part and the other into the imaginary part, then teasing them apart with circular even/odd symmetry. [PS8 solution pp. 3–4]

The exam’s ‘treasure chest’ filter asks for an order bound from a plotted response alone: count six extrema, invoke the polynomial-in-cosω limit, and conclude L≥5 without assuming Parks–McClellan. [Midterm pp. 10–11; solution pp. 8–9]

The midterm explicitly tells students that later parts may be solvable independently and grades understanding on an E/G/R/M/U scale, making reasoning more valuable than a lucky final value. [Midterm p. 1]

The lattice-expansion exam problem is a trap for brute force: replace z by z² and insert zero-reflection stages, so original coefficients simply occupy even lattice indices. [Midterm pp. 8–9; solution pp. 6–7]

Frequency-domain decimation of a 1024-point DFT folds the two 512-sample time halves together; frequency-domain expansion then creates two half-amplitude copies. This makes Fourier duality operational and testable. [Midterm pp. 12–13; solution pp. 10–11]
